domains.name: Academic Vocabulary
domains.summary: Academic Vocabulary covers the lexical platform for university study: the vocabulary size and text coverage needed to read and listen independently; the general academic, sub-technical and technical layers of university lexis; the word-level knowledge (morphology, word grammar, countability, spelling) needed for accurate production; and the strategies learners use to keep expanding vocabulary beyond the classroom. Academic word lists (AWL, AVL) are treated as useful but contested starting points, because the 'academic' status, meaning and frequency of items vary by discipline, and coverage thresholds are treated as approximate planning guides rather than cut-offs.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn which words are most worth your time for university study and how to learn and remember them. You will also practise using them accurately and precisely in writing and speech.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Secure the high-frequency base, word families and the vocabulary of university study and assignments, and establish independent learning routines with dictionaries and word cards.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Move academic and sub-technical vocabulary into accurate productive use within the student's discipline, including process verbs, evaluative lexis and discipline-specific senses.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Prioritise disciplinary terminology, lexical precision and evaluation for source-based writing on compressed one-year programmes.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Refine precision, shell nouns and evaluative lexis for research writing, using evidence from the target field's literature.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Check and secure the high-frequency base, then build general academic vocabulary, word families and command words for essay and exam tasks, with routines for inferring and recording new words.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Test rather than reteach the high-frequency base, and focus on academic and sub-technical vocabulary in the target discipline, evaluative lexis for critical reading and writing, and independent learning systems.

domains.name: Phraseology & Formulaic Language
domains.summary: Phraseology & Formulaic Language treats multi-word units — collocations, lexical bundles, spoken formulas and fixed expressions — as core carriers of academic meaning rather than decorative extras. Corpus research shows that expert academic writing and speech rely heavily on recurrent combinations whose functions differ (research-, text- and stance-oriented) and vary by discipline, and that student writers' use often differs from expert use in range and frequency (reported as underuse or overuse relative to a named reference corpus, not as error in itself). The domain also develops strategies (corpus consultation, critical use of phrase resources) so that learners can verify phraseology independently, while guarding against formulaic, template-driven text.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to notice and use the word combinations that academic writers and speakers rely on. You will also learn to check combinations yourself in dictionaries, collections of real texts and phrase lists.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build the habit of noticing and recording combinations, with frequent academic collocations and text-organising bundles from course materials.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Work on learners' own drafts: repair persistent miscollocations, reduce overused connectors and stance frames, and compare bundles with those in disciplinary texts.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Prioritise discipline-relevant collocations and bundles for source-based writing, checked against field texts in a compressed timeframe.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Profile the phraseology of target journals with self-built corpora and refine stance formulas for research writing and publication.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Build range in frequent academic collocations and text-organising bundles for essays and presentations, and introduce collocation dictionaries, error logs and guided phrasebank use.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Extend collocations into the research- and stance-oriented bundles met in research articles and needed for a source-based project, and introduce simple corpus searches to check usage in the target field.

domains.name: Register & Academic Style
domains.summary: Register & Academic Style develops learners' ability to read a communicative situation and choose language accordingly: register as a configuration of field, tenor and mode; the systematic differences in how speech and writing package meaning; and the features conventionally associated with formal academic prose. The domain deliberately treats style 'rules' as probabilistic tendencies to be tested against evidence of disciplinary and historical variation, frames impersonality as a choice about agency rather than a route to objectivity, and extends to inclusive language and to writing for non-specialist readers.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn why academic writing and speech sound as they do, and how to adjust your style for different readers. You will also learn to tell real conventions from over-simple 'rules'.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build register awareness through concrete contrasts (email, forum post, assignment) and an explicit, reasoned checklist of formality features, including precise rather than vague reference.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Reconcile conflicting module advice by examining disciplinary style, authorial presence and density in the student's own field and genres.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Calibrate density, impersonality and inclusive description for compressed source-based and professional writing, often in an unfamiliar discipline.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Align style with target journals and examiners' fields, claim contribution with appropriate presence, and write lay summaries and engagement texts for non-specialists.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Make formality features, precise reference and spoken–written differences explicit for essays and presentations, treating style advice as tendencies rather than absolute rules.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Move quickly from formality checklists to choices about authorial presence, information density and disciplinary style in source-based projects, testing prescriptive rules against texts from the target field.

domains.name: Academic Grammar
domains.summary: This domain covers the grammatical resources that carry meaning in academic registers, prioritised by what corpus research shows academic writing actually does rather than by a general-English syllabus order. Its centre of gravity is the noun phrase: academic prose compresses information into premodified and postmodified noun phrases and nominalisations far more than conversation does, so learners need both to unpack such phrases when reading and to build them when writing. Clause-level resources (tense, voice, modality, subordination, complement and reporting clauses) are treated in terms of the rhetorical choices they serve, such as currency in citation, agency in methods and degrees of commitment in claims. Accuracy topics are framed as monitoring and editing problems as much as knowledge problems, and the grammar of spoken academic interaction is treated on its own terms rather than measured against writing.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn the grammar academic texts use most, such as long noun phrases, tense and voice, and how it shapes your claims. You will also learn to find and fix your frequent errors.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Secure clause analysis, agreement, tense, the passive for process description, relative clauses and basic subordination with textbook-level texts, and introduce noun-phrase expansion and the grammar of discussion through description, definition and seminar tasks.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Consolidate tense, voice, articles and noun-phrase postmodification for essays and reports, introduce reporting structures for source-based writing, and build personal error monitoring tied to the progression assignment.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Assume most clause-level grammar and move quickly to phrasal complexity, nominalisation, reporting structures and tense in literature-based writing, with error monitoring geared to the extended project of the target programme.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Address grammar through students' disciplinary reading and assessed drafts, focusing on nominalisation, noun phrases, passive versus active choices and recurrent errors flagged in feedback.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Concentrate on tense in literature reviews, nominalisation, stance-bearing structures and editing efficiency under the time pressure of a short taught programme.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Refine information packaging (clefts, fronting, end-weight), voice and tense choices in research genres and independent self-editing for publication.

domains.name: Sentence Construction & Punctuation
domains.summary: This domain covers how clauses are combined into well-formed sentences, how punctuation marks grammatical structure and meaning, and how sentence-level choices (length, concision, end-weight) affect readability. Punctuation is treated as a consequence of clause and phrase analysis rather than as a list of rules, and conventions that vary by style guide (serial commas, quotation marks, capitalisation, title case) are taught as choices to be applied consistently. Sentence-level style is grounded in what corpus research shows about academic prose, in particular that its difficulty comes mainly from dense noun phrases rather than from long chains of clauses. The style of numbers and units in running text is covered with the language of quantity in num.number-expressions.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to build clear, correctly punctuated sentences and apply the conventions your department or style guide expects. You will also learn to edit sentences so readers can follow dense ideas.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Establish sentence types and boundaries, core comma use, apostrophes, capitals and basic quotation punctuation in short assignments, and introduce list formatting.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Consolidate boundary and punctuation accuracy under time pressure, including quotation punctuation for source-based essays, and introduce semicolons, colons and control of sentence length.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Assume basic boundary control and focus on concision for word-limited extended projects, semicolons and colons in dense prose, quotation conventions in literature-based writing and early work on end-weight.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Address the style-guide conventions departments require and sentence-level clarity in assessed reports and essays, with low-level mechanics handled through self-access.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on concision and end-weight in dissertations and data-heavy writing; mechanics are handled through proofreading checklists rather than taught sessions.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Refine sentence-level clarity, end-weight and house-style conventions for theses and journal submission.

domains.name: Cohesion & Coherence
domains.summary: This domain covers the resources that make a text hang together for its reader: cohesive ties (reference, conjunction, lexical cohesion) and the information-structuring choices (given–new order, thematic progression, encapsulation, text patterns) that make a sequence of sentences read as a purposeful whole. It treats cohesion as a means to coherence rather than a proxy for it, countering the connector-heavy, checklist approach that test preparation and some readings of learner-corpus findings tend to reinforce. Topics move from sentence-to-sentence linking towards text-level signalling and the reader-oriented explicitness that many English-medium academic readers expect; spoken signposting is covered in the presentation and listening domains.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how writers help readers follow their thinking: linking sentences, keeping key terms consistent and signalling where the text is going. More linking words alone do not make writing clear.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Foundation programmes concentrate on basic connectors, pronoun and noun reference and paragraph-level patterns, using short model texts and subject textbooks.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Undergraduate pre-sessional courses move learners from connector lists to selective, accurate linking and clear reference in essays and short reports, using the cohesion–coherence distinction to make sense of marking criteria.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Postgraduate pre-sessional courses add information flow, encapsulation with signalling nouns and reverse outlining, so that extended source-based projects read as one argument rather than a sequence of summaries.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Undergraduate in-sessional work diagnoses coherence problems in students' own assignments, especially reliance on connectors, unclear reference and weak transitions between paragraphs.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Taught postgraduate support focuses on dissertation-length coherence, terminological consistency and transitions between sections, and on using text patterns to read efficiently.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Doctoral writers refine flow in dense prose (thematic progression, encapsulation) and manage metatext and terminology across a thesis or article.

domains.name: Stance, Metadiscourse & Evaluation
domains.summary: This domain covers the interpersonal dimension of academic discourse: how writers and speakers signal certainty and commitment, evaluate ideas and sources, represent themselves, engage readers, and keep their own claims distinct from those they attribute to others. It draws on Hyland's models of metadiscourse and of stance and engagement and on Martin and White's appraisal framework, especially engagement, treating them as complementary lenses rather than a single taxonomy. Stance is approached as calibration and positioning grounded in evidence, not as lists of hedges to insert, and disciplinary variation is made explicit throughout.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to show how certain a claim is and to evaluate others' work fairly. You will also learn to show which ideas are yours and which come from sources.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Foundation programmes introduce basic hedging and boosting and bounded rather than sweeping generalisations, with simple opinion language in speech and writing.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Undergraduate pre-sessional courses focus on hedging and bounding generalisations, concession in argument essays, and keeping the writer's own claims distinct from source content.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Postgraduate pre-sessional courses add calibration of claims to evidence, evaluative language for critiquing studies and informed choices about self-mention, in preparation for literature-based assignments and research proposals.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Undergraduate in-sessional support helps students build an authorial voice in assignments, evaluate sources rather than describe them, and match stance conventions to their discipline.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Taught postgraduate support focuses on critical evaluation of literature, dialogic positioning in literature reviews and calibrated claims in dissertations.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Doctoral writers refine stance for publication: claiming contribution without over-claiming, positioning against the literature, managing self-mention and engaging expert readers.

domains.name: Rhetorical Functions
domains.summary: This domain covers recurrent rhetorical functions — defining, classifying, describing processes and structures, comparing, expressing cause and effect, exemplifying, explaining, hypothesising, recommending, summarising, narrating and evaluating — that cut across genres and disciplines. It follows the discourse approach to English for science and technology (Trimble), Mohan's knowledge framework and functional genre work (Martin and Rose; Nesi and Gardner's genre families), treating each function as a pairing of a communicative purpose with characteristic lexicogrammar and organisation. Functions are building blocks for paragraphs, sections and whole genres; teaching them through authentic disciplinary exemplars rather than decontextualised phrase lists keeps the focus on what each function achieves.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn the common jobs that academic texts do — such as defining a term, comparing two approaches, explaining why something happens or recommending action — and the language and organisation each job needs.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Foundation programmes teach the core functions (defining, classifying, describing processes, comparing, cause and effect, exemplifying) through subject content, often in science, engineering and business contexts.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Undergraduate pre-sessional courses consolidate comparing, cause and effect and explaining, and combine them with problem–solution and evaluation in expository and argument essays and short reports.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Postgraduate pre-sessional courses emphasise criterion-based evaluation, defining contested or operational terms and hypothesising, in preparation for critical reviews, research proposals and dissertation-style projects.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Undergraduate in-sessional support targets the functions demanded by specific assignments and genre families, such as explanation, critique and case study.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Taught postgraduate support emphasises contested and operational definitions, criterion-based evaluation, explanation of results and recommendations in dissertations and reports.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Doctoral writers mainly revisit hypothesising, defining contested constructs and explaining results within research genres.

domains.name: Reading Processes & Fluency
domains.summary: This domain covers the cognitive and linguistic foundations of academic reading: automatic word recognition, parsing of compressed academic sentences, reading fluency and volume, and the way these lower-level processes interact with background knowledge, purpose and reading load. L2 reading research finds that L2 vocabulary and grammatical knowledge are the strongest correlates of L2 reading comprehension, so the domain prioritises building the linguistic base and reading volume on which strategies depend rather than treating strategies as a substitute for them. It also addresses the practical conditions of university reading: on-screen texts, long reading lists and the legitimate, checked use of a reader's other languages, and accessible formats such as text-to-speech.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how reading works and why more words and more reading make everything easier. You will practise reading fluently, coping with long reading lists, reading on screen and using your other languages.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build automaticity and reading volume through extensive reading of graded and accessible texts, alongside explicit work on reading purpose, background knowledge and short complex sentences.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Diagnose each learner's vocabulary size and reading rate early, set realistic fluency targets with easy texts, and teach purpose-setting and sentence parsing with textbook and general academic prose.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Focus on parsing dense disciplinary prose, building background knowledge for learners changing field, and planning realistic loads of authentic articles read largely on screen.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Focus on coping with module reading lists, dense textbook and article prose, and strategic, transparent use of other languages and translation tools.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Emphasise triage of large reading loads on compressed timelines, deliberate background-knowledge building for students changing discipline, and efficient on-screen reading.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Address sustainable reading of large literatures, realistic rate expectations for specialist and theoretical texts, and the place of plurilingual reading in research.

domains.name: Reading Strategies & Comprehension
domains.summary: This domain covers the strategies and comprehension skills that turn decoded text into usable understanding: previewing, selective reading, identifying main ideas and text organisation, tracking reference and stance, inferring, monitoring and repairing comprehension, annotating, and integrating prose with visuals. Strategy instruction has positive but variable average effects, and its benefits depend on learners having enough language knowledge to apply strategies to the text at hand. Skimming and scanning are often over-represented in materials shaped by test formats relative to the careful reading for learning and argument that dominates university study, so the domain gives priority to main ideas, structure, reference and stance, and treats speeded strategies as tools for specific purposes.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to get an overview of a text, follow its main ideas, structure and references, and work out whose view is expressed. You will also learn to notice and fix gaps in understanding.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Prioritise previewing, paragraph structure, main ideas, reference tracking and textbook reading, with skimming and scanning practised as purposeful tools on accessible texts.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Make main ideas, text organisation and the status of claims the assessed core, using textbook chapters and accessible academic articles, and avoid test-driven over-emphasis on skimming and scanning.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Make research-article navigation and the reading of writer stance the assessed core, using articles from learners' target fields, and treat skimming and scanning as revision.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Apply strategies to disciplinary textbooks and early encounters with research articles, with emphasis on stance, inference and visuals.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on research-article navigation, stance and efficient previewing of large numbers of sources.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Address fine-grained stance reading, comprehension monitoring with specialist texts and efficient navigation of research literature.

domains.name: Critical & Multiple-Text Reading
domains.summary: This domain addresses reading as evaluation and integration: reconstructing arguments, evaluating evidence and methods, surfacing assumptions and perspective, reading theoretical texts, reading across multiple sources and mapping literatures, and moving from comprehension to a reasoned response; reading for a specific writing task is covered by the reading-to-write topic in the Writing strand, and the general habit of critical questioning by the Critical Thinking domain. Critical reading is presented as questioning and evaluating rather than fault-finding, and as partly discipline-specific; the notion of critical thinking is itself contested in EAP. Research on multiple-document reading shows that attending to sources and integrating across texts are distinct skills that do not develop automatically from single-text comprehension.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to judge the arguments and evidence in what you read, notice assumptions and perspectives, and compare sources. You will then form your own reasoned response.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Introduce critical reading through accessible argumentative texts, focusing on finding the argument, asking critical questions and writing short reasoned responses.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Make argument identification and the summary–response the assessed core, using short argumentative and textbook-style sources on general academic topics.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Make evidence evaluation, stance and integration across several sources the assessed core of an extended source-based project, with an introduction to reading empirical studies and mapping a small literature.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Apply critical reading to disciplinary sources, including multiple texts and empirical studies, with attention to evidence, assumptions and perspective.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Emphasise methods critique, multiple-text integration and literature mapping for assignments and the dissertation.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Focus on mapping and positioning within a literature, reading theoretical texts and critiquing methods at a specialist level.

domains.name: Lecture & Academic Listening
domains.summary: Academic listening is modelled here as two interacting sets of processes: decoding, which turns the acoustic signal into words and clauses in real time, and meaning-building, which relates what has been decoded to context, discourse structure, speaker purpose and prior knowledge. The domain moves from perceptual topics (connected speech, segmentation, speech rate, accent) through lecture discourse (phases, organisational and relevance markers, main points, stance) to the settings in which students listen (live and recorded lectures, seminars, briefings, academic media), with metacognitive strategy running throughout. Listening is treated as something to be taught, not only tested, and accent variation is treated as normal in international universities rather than as deviation from a single native-speaker norm. Deaf and hard-of-hearing students, and others who rely on captions, transcripts or note-taking support, may show these skills through other modes, and tasks should allow for this.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn why natural speech can be hard to catch and practical ways to follow the structure, key points and viewpoints of lectures, seminars and recorded talks.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build decoding of connected speech and confidence with short, clearly signposted lecture extracts on accessible content, together with simple preparation routines.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Move from short decoding work to full-length authentic lectures on first-year content, with explicit work on discourse and relevance markers and main-point selection, assessed through lecture notes and listening-into-writing tasks.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Assume basic lecture decoding and work with dense, discipline-related lectures and recorded seminars, focusing on relevance marking, speaker stance on contested material and following peer discussion.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Use students' own module lectures and recordings to diagnose specific decoding or discourse problems and build independent review strategies.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on dense, fast-paced specialist lectures, seminar discussion among peers from many language backgrounds, and inferring lecturer stance on contested material.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Address research seminars, conference talks, podcasts and multi-party discussion, where speakers are specialists with varied accents who signpost less explicitly.

domains.name: Note-taking & Note-making
domains.summary: The domain treats note-taking (recording from lectures in real time) and note-making (building notes from reading and from later review) as distinct but connected practices. Following Kiewra (1985), notes serve both an encoding function, through the processing involved in taking them, and an external-storage function for later review, and the review function often matters more; the domain therefore covers selection, shorthand and format, lecture and reading notes, review, digital tools and collaboration. Claims about particular formats, or about longhand versus laptop notes, are presented with their evidential limits.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to take notes that capture the key ideas of lectures and readings, record where each idea came from, and use your notes to revise and write.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Establish selection, abbreviation and simple formats with short, well-structured inputs, and link notes from reading to avoiding unintentional plagiarism.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Develop real-time lecture notes with explicit selection criteria and formats, and source-tracked reading notes, feeding integrated listening- and reading-into-writing assessments.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Concentrate on source-tracked notes from longer, multiple readings that separate quotation, paraphrase and comment and are organised by theme to feed synthesis and the extended project.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Work with students' own lecture and reading notes, focusing on review through self-testing and on informed choices of tools.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Manage heavy reading loads with source-tracked, thematically organised notes that support synthesis and the dissertation.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Note-making shifts towards literature management and research records; reading notes that keep source and own words strictly apart remain central.

domains.name: Seminars & Discussion
domains.summary: Seminars, tutorials and discussion groups are where students are expected to co-construct understanding of readings and ideas in real time, and where participation is often assessed formally or informally. This domain treats discussion as negotiated, multi-turn interaction rather than a list of functional phrases: learners need to prepare substantively, find and hold turns, state and justify positions, explain concepts and readings to peers, mitigate disagreement, build on and summarise others' contributions and, at higher levels, facilitate. Participation is also shaped by anxiety, positioning, disability and the way tutors and peers distribute the floor, so the domain addresses the conditions for participation as well as individual skill, and accepts more than one mode of contribution, including written and chat contributions.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how university discussions work, how to prepare and join in, and how to make, support and explain your points. You will also learn to respond to others and help discussions move forward.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Make seminar purposes and participation expectations explicit, and build reliable resources for giving views, asking questions and checking understanding through short, well-prepared, low-stakes discussions on accessible content.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Move from rehearsed phrases to extended discussion of set readings, with explicit work on preparation, giving and justifying views, turn-taking and mitigated disagreement, often in an assessed seminar that informs progression.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Prepare for postgraduate seminars in which contribution may be assessed from the first weeks, emphasising critical engagement with readings, citing sources in speech, explaining concepts to mixed-discipline peers and taking the floor in fast discussion.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Embed practice in learners' own modules, focusing on subject-specific expectations, entering fast discussions with peers who share local references, and building on others' points.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Emphasise critical engagement with readings, citing in speech, facilitating and summarising in intensive one-year programmes where seminar contribution may be assessed from the first weeks.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Focus on research group meetings, reading groups and peer seminars on work in progress, where researchers question, critique and are questioned as emerging members of a discipline.

domains.name: Presentations
domains.summary: Academic presentations range from short assessed talks on foundation and pre-sessional programmes to conference papers, posters, research seminars and short-format pitches at doctoral level. This domain treats the presentation as a spoken, multimodal genre designed for listeners who process information once, in real time: it needs explicit structure and signposting, visuals that support rather than duplicate speech, intelligible prosody and a delivery mode between reading a script and improvising. It gives particular attention to the interactive phases — openings, question-and-answer sessions and poster conversations — which research on conference presentations shows are central to how presenters engage audiences and establish credibility, and it treats poster design as part of the poster genre.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to plan, design and deliver presentations that listeners can follow, explain visuals and data, and handle questions. Tasks range from short class talks to posters, research talks and pitches.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build clear structure, signposting, delivery from notes and basic slide design through short, rehearsed presentations, often in groups, on accessible topics.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Develop clear, well-structured individual presentations on a researched topic, with audible signposting, intelligible delivery and short questions, often as part of progression assessment.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Develop presentations that use sources and data for mixed-discipline audiences, with emphasis on explaining visuals, adapting to the audience and handling challenging questions, and, for research-degree entrants, presenting a proposal.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support module-specific presentation tasks, including group presentations and recorded assessments, with attention to disciplinary expectations and audience.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on presenting projects and dissertation plans, explaining data, handling challenging questions and working in recorded or online formats.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Address research seminars, conference papers, posters, progression presentations and short-format pitches within strict time limits, framing contribution for specialist and mixed audiences and engaging productively in discussion sessions.

domains.name: Pronunciation & Fluency
domains.summary: The domain adopts the intelligibility principle (Levis, 2005): the goal is speech that listeners can understand with reasonable effort, not a native-like accent. Building on Munro and Derwing's (1995) distinction between accentedness, comprehensibility and intelligibility, priority goes to the features most likely to affect understanding in academic speaking — word stress in academic vocabulary, thought groups and prominence, intonation for discourse functions, high-functional-load segmentals — together with fluency and repair. Pronunciation is linked to listening, since perception supports production, and to the presentations, seminars and teaching in which students use it; accent is treated as part of speakers' identity rather than as an error to be removed. Listeners share responsibility for understanding, so assessment should judge intelligibility rather than accentedness, and speakers who stammer or have other speech differences should not be assessed against fluency norms they cannot meet.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn which features of pronunciation most affect whether listeners understand you, and practise them in presentations and seminars. Your goal is to be understood, not to change your accent.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Establish intelligibility as the goal, with focused work on word stress, thought groups and each learner's own highest-priority sounds.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Integrate word stress, thought groups and prominence with presentation and seminar speaking, using recordings, listener transcription and peer feedback to set individual goals.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Apply prominence, intonation and technical-term pronunciation to explaining specialist content and data in presentations and seminars, preparing for postgraduate presenting and, for some, teaching.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Provide short, targeted support for assessed presentations and technical vocabulary, usually through individual feedback.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on specialist terms, numbers and data in speech, and on fluent delivery of dense content within strict time limits.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Support conference presentations, vivas and teaching (for example as graduate teaching assistants), where prosody affects how clearly explanations come across to audiences.

domains.name: Group Work & Collaboration
domains.summary: Group projects, assessed group presentations and collaborative reports are common across disciplines, yet students often receive little guidance on how to collaborate, and multilingual students can be positioned as less competent and allocated marginal roles. This domain covers why universities assess collaboration and how groups plan and allocate work, run meetings, negotiate disagreement, write together, and document and evaluate contributions. It treats equitable participation as a shared responsibility of all group members and of course design, not as a deficit of particular students.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to plan group projects, run meetings, handle disagreement and write together. You will also learn to show what each member contributed and to make sure everyone can take part.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Introduce the purposes of group work, simple role allocation and meeting routines through scaffolded projects with explicit ground rules and teacher monitoring.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Use short group projects and group presentations to practise planning, meeting language and inclusive participation, in preparation for the assessed group work common in first-year undergraduate modules.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Prepare for intensive, highly multilingual taught-postgraduate group assignments by practising fast role negotiation, meeting management and documenting contributions for peer-moderated marks, often within one short project.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support assessed group projects with meeting management, conflict handling, collaborative writing workflows and peer evaluation of contributions.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Address intensive, often highly multilingual group assignments in which students must quickly establish roles, resolve disagreements and document contributions for peer-moderated marks.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Focus on research-team meetings, co-authoring and documenting contributions, linking collaboration to authorship norms and professional conduct.

domains.name: Writing Process
domains.summary: Covers how academic texts are produced rather than what they look like: representing coursework and exam tasks, generating and organising content, drafting, writing from sources, and managing time, language choice and affect across extended projects. It draws on cognitive process models (Flower & Hayes, 1981; Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1987) and L2 composing research (Zamel, 1983), which show that skilled writers plan, draft and review recursively and use writing to develop ideas. Hyland (2003) argues that process pedagogy needs to be complemented by explicit attention to genre and reader expectations, so these topics should be taught alongside PAR, ESS and the genre strands rather than as a free-standing ‘process approach’.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to turn a brief or exam question into a plan and draft, write from your reading, use all your languages, and manage long projects.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Make the process visible: task analysis, idea generation and outlining for short assignments, with plans and drafts submitted and discussed before the final text.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Rehearse the full cycle on an extended essay: analysing the brief, reading to write from a small set of sources, drafting from notes and working to a word budget.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Use a larger source-based project, often modelled on a literature-based assignment or dissertation proposal, to practise question-driven reading, scoping, milestone planning and drafting from extensive notes.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Apply process strategies to learners' own module assignments, with emphasis on interpreting briefs, juggling deadlines and integrating disciplinary reading.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Compress the cycle for dense, short-turnaround master's assignments and plan ahead for the dissertation.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Treat writing as a way of thinking and as sustained practice: routines, milestones, writing blocks and plurilingual composing across a multi-year project.

domains.name: Paragraph Development
domains.summary: Covers the paragraph as the main unit through which academic writers develop and support a point: controlling ideas, support and analysis, internal coherence, closure, division, paragraph functions and the integration of sources. Paragraph scaffolds such as topic-sentence models and PEEL are useful entry points for foundation and undergraduate-entry pre-sessional writers, but expert paragraphs vary considerably (Braddock, 1974), so teaching should move learners from templates towards functional judgements about what a paragraph needs to do in its context. Coherence is better taught through information flow and logical relations than through connector lists (Crossley & McNamara, 2012).
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to build paragraphs that make one clear point, support it with explanation and evidence, and use sources while keeping your own voice.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build secure control of the controlling idea, support and closure, using scaffolds such as PEEL explicitly as temporary supports.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Teach paragraph scaffolds (PEEL, topic and concluding sentences) explicitly, then withdraw them as learners move to source-based paragraphs in which their own point leads.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Revisit scaffolds only where diagnosis shows a need; focus on multi-source paragraphs in which the writer's point leads, evidence is evaluated and paragraphing follows function rather than formula.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Diagnose paragraph-level problems in disciplinary assignments, especially description without analysis and breaks in internal coherence.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on dense, multi-source paragraphs and on flexible paragraphing that serves the argument rather than a formula.

domains.name: Essay Construction
domains.summary: Covers how an essay is built around a central argument: structure, thesis, introductions, body organisation, conclusions, depth of focus, criticality, headings and titles; essay types are treated under ges.genre-families and answering the question set under wpr.task-analysis. The essay is a major assessed genre in many humanities and social science programmes but is only one of many genre families in university writing (Nesi & Gardner, 2012), and the five-paragraph essay taught in many schools and test-preparation courses is a scaffold that does not match university essays in length, structure or source use (Caplan & Johns, 2019; Moore & Morton, 2005). Teaching should centre on argument (Wingate, 2012) and treat structural templates as means to that end.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to plan and build an essay around a clear, well-supported position that answers the question, from thesis and introduction to body, conclusion and title.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Introduce thesis-led essay structure with scaffolds, moving from short opinion-based essays to short source-based ones.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Move from short essays to extended source-based essays with an explicit thesis, thematic body and evaluative conclusion, using structural scaffolds first and then unlearning test-driven templates.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Assume basic essay structure; concentrate on scope, criticality and thematic organisation of a larger reading base, and on how essay expectations vary across target departments and countries.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Work with disciplinary essay types, answering the specific question, choosing depth over breadth and demonstrating criticality.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on criticality, scope and argument in short, dense essays and on discipline-specific conventions such as headings.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Carry argument structure and title-writing skills into articles and thesis chapters; essays themselves are less central.

domains.name: Revising, Editing & Proofreading
domains.summary: Covers how writers improve drafts: distinguishing revision of argument and structure from sentence-level editing and surface proofreading, and the techniques, feedback sources, tools and ethical limits involved. Sommers (1980) found that inexperienced writers tend to treat revision as rewording, so teaching should put global revision and criteria-based self-assessment before editing. The value of written corrective feedback has been contested (Truscott, 1996; Ferris, 1999), but meta-analytic evidence suggests it can improve accuracy (Kang & Han, 2015); learners therefore need routines for targeted self-editing, trained peer review (Lundstrom & Baker, 2009) and critical use of automated tools (see dig.automated-feedback-tools) and of the third-party help their institution permits, which varies between countries and institutions.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to improve drafts in stages: argument and structure first, then sentences, then surface errors. You will also learn to use criteria, peer feedback, tools and proofreaders within the rules.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Establish the difference between revising and correcting, basic self-editing routines and structured, supported peer review.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Build multi-draft cycles in which global revision comes before editing, with structured peer review and personal error logs for the accuracy that progression assessment usually rewards.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Compress the cycle for writers who may already draft fluently: prioritise global revision and criteria-based self-assessment of a source-based project, and agree what proofreading and AI help the programme permits.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Apply revision strategies to module assignments and use tools and proofreading support within institutional rules.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on efficient global revision under time pressure and on critical use of editing and AI tools.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Revise long texts with reverse outlining and supervisor and peer feedback, edit for style at publication level, and understand the rules on editorial help with theses and articles.

domains.name: Information Literacy & Source Evaluation
domains.summary: Covers how scholarly knowledge is produced and published, how learners turn an assignment topic into a searchable question, how they search catalogues and databases, and how they judge whether a source is trustworthy and fit for a specific purpose. Evaluation is treated as contextual judgement, in line with the ACRL frame 'Authority Is Constructed and Contextual', rather than as checklist compliance, and lateral reading is included as an empirically grounded alternative to judging a site on its own terms. The language demands are real: generating search terms draws on vocabulary depth and disciplinary terminology, and judging a source depends on reading its genre signals and paratext.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how academic work is published, how to find sources with library tools, and how to judge whether a source is reliable enough for your purpose.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Distinguishing scholarly from popular sources, simple catalogue and discovery-tool searches, and basic credibility checks, including lateral reading of web sources.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Subject databases, citation chaining from key readings, and module-specific judgements about what counts as an acceptable source.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Efficient, documented searching for dissertations, checking venues and retractions, and legitimate access to paywalled work.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Systematic or scoping searching, comprehensive citation chaining, verification of venues and article status, and reproducible search records maintained across a multi-year project.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Telling source types apart, focusing a set essay title into a searchable question, and judging which sources tutors will accept in an extended essay.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Database searching with concept tables and Boolean strings for a project in the destination discipline, evaluating empirical studies for fitness of purpose, and keeping search records.

domains.name: Summarising, Paraphrasing & Quoting
domains.summary: Covers the core textual practices by which writers bring others' words and ideas into their own texts: quoting, paraphrasing and summarising, the reporting language that attributes and evaluates source content, and the signalling that keeps the writer's voice distinct from the sources'. The domain follows research suggesting that source-use problems in L2 writing are often developmental, linked to comprehension, vocabulary and an incomplete sense of why sources are used, rather than to intent to deceive (Howard; Pecorari; Shi; Keck). Instruction therefore pairs language work with purpose: learners transform sources in order to serve their own argument, and close dependence on source wording is treated as something to be taught through, not only policed.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to quote, paraphrase and summarise sources accurately, to report what other writers say precisely, and to make clear which ideas are yours and which come from sources.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Accurate quotation, basic signal phrases and neutral reporting verbs, summarising paragraphs and early paraphrasing, with close dependence on source wording treated as a normal stage to work through.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Disciplinary norms for quotation and citation form, summarising whole texts, and source use that serves analysis rather than display.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid, accurate summarising of research articles, evaluative reporting, and clear voice boundaries in dense, multi-source writing.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Fine control of reporting verbs, citation form and attribution in research writing, and transparent use of sources in other languages.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Accurate quotation, passage summary, paraphrase written from understanding, and signal phrases with continued attribution in assessed essays.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Paraphrasing and summarising whole research articles, stance-bearing reporting verbs and clear voice boundaries in source-based assignments for the destination discipline.

domains.name: Synthesis
domains.summary: Covers discourse synthesis: building a new text that integrates several sources around the writer's own organising ideas rather than summarising them one by one. The domain moves from the concept of synthesis, through tools for organising sources (matrices and thematic grouping), to the language of relating sources, identifying gaps and tensions, and writing synthesis paragraphs, and includes integrated reading- and listening-into-writing tasks in coursework, progression assessment and proficiency tests. Spivey's account of synthesis as organising, selecting and connecting, together with research on integrated writing (Plakans; Plakans and Gebril; Grabe and Zhang), frames synthesis as a constructive reading–writing process rather than a set of linking phrases.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to bring several sources together around your own ideas, show how they agree or differ, and complete tasks that combine reading, listening and writing.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Understanding synthesis versus serial summary, simple matrices built from two or three sources, and short integrated tasks.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Synthesising module readings in essays and literature review assignments, with explicit relationships between sources and, in final-year projects, identification of gaps.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Literature reviews that group sources by theme, relate them critically and identify gaps that justify a dissertation question.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Synthesising large, contested literatures and articulating tensions and gaps that position an original contribution.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Understanding synthesis as opposed to serial summary in extended essays, and integrated reading-into-writing tasks used for progression decisions.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Relating sources explicitly and writing synthesis paragraphs for literature-based assignments, with timed integrated tasks and early gap statements for project proposals.

domains.name: Citation & Referencing
domains.summary: Citation is both a technical system and a rhetorical practice. This domain moves from why and when academics cite, through the mechanics of the main referencing systems (author–date, numeric and note-based), locators and reference lists, to the jobs sources and citations do in an argument, how citation varies across disciplines, and whose knowledge citation and indexing practices make visible. Formatting is treated as learnable and checkable, ideally with reference-management tools, so that teaching time goes to the harder judgements: what needs citing, whether a cited source really supports the claim, how citation positions the writer, what disciplinary readers expect, and which perspectives a reference list leaves out.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn why and when to cite, how to format citations and reference lists in your department's system, how to use sources to build your argument, and how to choose whose work you cite.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Why and when to cite, and accurate author–date (or departmental) citations and reference lists for books, articles and web pages.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Consistent author–date citation, reference lists and locators across an extended source-based essay, with sources used to support and contrast ideas, often assessed for progression.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Checking citations for accuracy and fidelity, using sources to compare, evaluate and link ideas in a literature-based project, and a first look at the citation system and practices of the target discipline.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Switching to the department's prescribed system, citing a wider range of source types, and using citation for more than attribution in disciplinary assignments.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Using citation to compare, evaluate and position sources in critical reviews and dissertations, matching disciplinary norms, and considering whose scholarship a literature review draws on.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Switching between journal styles, managing large reference libraries accurately, positioning a contribution within a field, and making deliberate choices about whose work is cited.

domains.name: Academic Integrity
domains.summary: Academic integrity is taught here as values and practices rather than a list of offences. The domain moves from shared values and an informed understanding of plagiarism (including the developmental status of patchwriting and the contested role of intention) to collusion, contract cheating, reuse of one's own work and research integrity, and to the procedural knowledge learners need: interpreting similarity reports, navigating policies and processes, knowing their procedural rights, and managing pressure without shortcuts. Rules differ between institutions and modules, so teaching centres on locating and reading the rules that apply. Similarity and AI-detection scores are never treated as verdicts, the burden of establishing misconduct lies with the institution, and institutions share responsibility for the conditions (clear briefs, workable deadlines, accessible support) in which integrity is possible.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn what academic integrity means, how to avoid plagiarism and collusion, and what similarity reports show. You will learn where to find help under pressure, and your rights if your work is questioned.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Values, a clear and non-threatening understanding of plagiarism and collusion, and where to get help, introduced early in the course.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Plagiarism and patchwriting in source-based essays, formative use of similarity reports, collusion in group tasks, and the policies and rights that will apply in undergraduate study.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Plagiarism, citation fidelity and AI use in extended postgraduate writing, how similarity reports and integrity processes work, learners' procedural rights, and a first look at research integrity and reuse of one's own work.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Department-specific rules on collaboration, reuse of work and lab or project data, and strategies for managing workload pressure.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid orientation to regulations, reuse of prior work, group-assessment boundaries, and integrity in dissertation research and data.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Research integrity, text recycling in theses and publications, authorship, and the codes of conduct governing research.

domains.name: Critical Thinking
domains.summary: This domain treats critical thinking as a contested, partly discipline-specific set of practices and dispositions — questioning, weighing evidence, recognising inference patterns and their limits, considering perspectives fairly and reflecting on one's own position — that can be made explicit and taught. It rejects the deficit framing that some groups of learners 'cannot think critically': hesitancy to critique published work is common among novice writers of all backgrounds and is treated as a matter of assessment genres, novice status and licence to question, not as a cognitive or cultural deficit. The domain supplies the reasoning that the Academic Argumentation domain turns into written and spoken argument.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn what tutors mean by 'be critical', how to question and weigh evidence and reasoning, and how to notice common errors in thinking, including your own.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Make criticality concrete with familiar topics: description versus analysis, simple questions about evidence, and fair representation of different views.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Connect critical moves to progression tasks: questioning sources, moving from description to analysis, and representing views fairly in source-based essays and seminars.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Recalibrate to postgraduate criticality: decode 'be more critical' feedback, question research evidence and designs, and evaluate sources for literature-based assignments.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Embed criticality in disciplinary tasks with module exemplars, especially during the first-year transition when 'be more critical' feedback first appears.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Accelerate recalibration to master's-level expectations: evaluating research designs, competing theories and contested literatures from the first assignment.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Focus on evaluating and positioning theory, reflexivity, and the epistemological commitments of one's own research.

domains.name: Academic Argumentation
domains.summary: This domain treats argument as the organising purpose of most assessed academic writing and much academic talk: taking a position, supporting claims with evidence and explicit reasoning, anticipating and answering objections, and sequencing sub-claims into a cumulative case. Hirvela (2017) argues that L2 writing pedagogy has given argumentation less attention than its centrality warrants, and Wingate (2012) found that students often receive feedback on 'argument' without being shown what it consists of. Toulmin's model, argumentation schemes and argument mapping are offered as analytical tools rather than templates, and disciplinary variation in what counts as a good argument (Andrews, 2010) is made explicit.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn what an academic argument is, how to build one from claims, evidence and reasoning, and how to answer other views fairly in writing and discussion.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build the concept of argument as a supported position, with simple claim–evidence–explanation links in short essays and talks, and awareness of how texts persuade.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Develop a clear, qualified position in the source-based essays used for progression, with counter-argument and concession, and carry these moves into seminar discussion.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Prepare for postgraduate study by sustaining a position across longer source-based assignments, conceding and rebutting with evidence, and evaluating the arguments of research articles.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Adapt argument to disciplinary genres, make reasoning explicit for subject readers, and evaluate others' arguments in readings, critiques and dissertations.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Construct extended, evidence-dense arguments in assignments and dissertations, making warrants explicit for expert readers and evaluating research arguments.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Sustain a thesis-length argument, position it within scholarly debates and defend it orally in supervision, conferences and the viva.

domains.name: Essay & Examination Genres
domains.summary: This domain covers the essay, examination, review and source-based genres most often assessed in foundation, pre-sessional and taught programmes, including the extended source-based project that caps many pre-sessional and foundation courses, together with the genre concepts and analytic strategies learners need to handle genres they have not been explicitly taught. Comparison, explanation and problem–solution essays are treated as rhetorical patterns within the essay family rather than as separate genres, and each genre topic integrates component skills from the writing, sources, argument, discourse and reading strands. Because conventions vary by discipline, department and assignment brief, every topic stresses analysis of local exemplars, briefs and marking criteria rather than a single template; the domain draws on the ESP, Sydney School and New Rhetoric genre traditions and on corpus evidence about genre families in UK student writing.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn what different kinds of university writing are for, how they are organised and what language they use, and how to study examples so you can handle new tasks.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Discussion and expository essays, summary–response and short answers with strong scaffolding, building towards a guided extended source-based project and the idea that texts are shaped by purpose and reader.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: The move from test-style opinion essays to source-based argumentative essays and annotated bibliographies, culminating in the extended project, with a map of the genre families met in the first year of a degree.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Source-based argument, article critiques and annotated bibliographies feeding an extended project with a short review of literature, plus independent analysis of exemplars from the target master's programme.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Discipline-specific essays, exam essays, critiques and reflective writing worked through real module briefs, criteria and feedback, with coursework literature reviews in later years.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid adaptation to coursework literature reviews, critiques, reflective and exam genres within a compressed year, with independent genre analysis as the transferable skill.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Genre analysis as an independent research skill and book reviews as early publications; doctoral genres themselves sit in the Research Communication strand.

domains.name: Report & Practice-Based Genres
domains.summary: This domain covers report-based, practice-based and professional genres in which students document investigations, analyse cases, justify designs, propose projects, summarise for decision-makers, reflect on practice and write for non-academic readers. Most are discipline-specific in their sections, terminology and evidence, so each topic sets out common purposes, stages and language while stressing that lab manuals, templates, handbooks and assignment briefs override any generic model. The domain draws on genre-family research on UK student writing, analyses of particular student genres such as the lab report and the business case report, and research on reflective writing.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how reports, case studies, proposals, portfolios and dissertations work and what their readers need, and how to follow your own department's templates and expectations.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Report conventions, guided lab reports and introductory case studies and business reports in subject pathways.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Report conventions and, in subject-specific strands, short lab, case or business reports; the extended project may itself take report form.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Report formats for the target discipline, such as business, case or small empirical project reports, and in some programmes a short taught-programme project proposal.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Discipline-embedded lab, design, business and case reports, placement portfolios and the final-year dissertation or project.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: The dissertation proposal and the master's dissertation, alongside professional reports, case analyses, policy briefs and portfolios, often within a compressed timeline.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Policy briefs and public-facing writing for engagement and impact; doctoral proposals and theses sit in the Research Communication strand.

domains.name: Research Writing
domains.summary: Research Writing covers the part-genres, macrostructures and practices through which postgraduate and early-career writers report and position their own research: introductions built on CARS-type moves, literature reviews, framework and methods sections, results, discussions, conclusions, abstracts, theses (including theses by publication), proposals, systematic and scoping reviews, and research instruments. Move analyses (Swales 1990, 2004; Kanoksilapatham 2005; Yang & Allison 2003; Kwan 2006) are descriptive models to test against disciplinary exemplars, not templates, and IMRaD is dominant in experimental fields but far from universal. The domain also covers the sociopragmatic and self-regulatory work of doctoral candidature, such as supervision, progression reviews, teaching as a graduate teaching assistant, sustaining output and writing reflexively, which Kamler and Thomson (2014) treat as both text work and identity work.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how dissertations, theses and research articles are organised in your field and how to write each part. You will also prepare for doctoral progress reviews and for teaching.

stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Not normally taught as research writing: undergraduate-entry courses build the report, summary and essay skills it later draws on, and any project abstract can use the core abstract moves.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Focus on how research articles are organised (IMRaD and its variants), short introductions that establish a gap, research questions and instrument wording for small projects and, for prospective doctoral students, the research proposal.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support final-year projects and dissertations with methods, results, discussion and abstract writing, anchored in departmental exemplars and the module's own reporting conventions.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Treat the master's dissertation as the main site: research questions and the gap, the literature review as argument, methods and results, calibrated discussion and the abstract, with structured reviews, instruments and ethics documents where the design requires them.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Move to thesis macrostructure and theses by publication, framework chapters, introductions and claims of contribution, progression reviews, supervision, teaching as a graduate teaching assistant and the sustained drafting of a long document.

domains.name: Publication & Dissemination
domains.summary: Publication & Dissemination covers the genres, practices and politics through which research reaches readers and is examined and funded: the publishing process, journal choice, the occluded genres around submission (cover letters, reviewer reports, responses to reviewers), open-research statements, conference abstracts and conference participation, the doctoral viva and thesis corrections, turning theses into articles, authorship and contributorship, funding applications, public engagement and academic self-presentation, including personal statements for postgraduate study. Many of these genres are hidden from novices because they are rarely published, so making exemplars and expectations visible is central to teaching. The domain also addresses the opportunities and inequities multilingual scholars meet in English-medium publishing (Flowerdew 1999; Lillis & Curry 2010) and treats them as structural issues, not individual deficits.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how research gets published, examined and funded, and how to write and speak in the texts and events involved, from cover letters to conference questions.

stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Focus on personal statements and short academic CVs for postgraduate applications, with a brief introduction to how research is published for students considering research careers.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Introduce the publishing process, authorship, conference abstracts and open-research requirements, and support doctoral and scholarship applications for students planning research careers.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Make this the core: publishing and peer review in both roles, conference participation, turning thesis chapters into articles, the viva and corrections, funding applications, engagement, and the politics of publishing in English.

domains.name: Data Commentary & Visuals
domains.summary: Data commentary is where numerical and visual evidence becomes argument: learners must read visuals accurately, select what matters, and write or speak about it with claims calibrated to the evidence rather than exhaustive description. The domain runs from visual literacy (visual types, reading graphs and tables, recognising misleading displays) through the lexicogrammar of trends, proportions and diagrams, to the genre of data commentary and the conventions for labelling, referring to and creating visuals. Test description tasks, such as IELTS Academic Writing Task 1, are treated as a contrast case: it rewards selective description of key features, whereas university data commentary also interprets, explains, compares and qualifies.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to read graphs, tables and diagrams accurately and describe them precisely. You will also use visuals as evidence in your writing and create clear, honest visuals of your own.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Reading common graphs and tables and describing trends, proportions and processes precisely, using visuals from subject modules such as business, science and engineering.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Accurate graph reading and trend and proportion language, moving towards short commentaries that select and interpret rather than describe every value.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Data commentary that locates, highlights, interprets and qualifies findings, typically assessed in an extended project report, with secure in-text reference to visuals.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Data commentary, captions and in-text references in lab, project and business reports, and creating charts from learners’ own data.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Commenting on results in dissertations with appropriately hedged interpretation, and critically evaluating visuals in sources.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Data commentary in results and discussion chapters and articles, figures designed to journal requirements, and visual argument in research presentations.

domains.name: Academic Numeracy Language
domains.summary: Academic numeracy language is the lexicogrammar and conceptual precision needed to talk and write about quantities, measurements, statistics and mathematical relations in English. Errors here are rarely ‘just language’: confusing per cent with percentage points, using ‘significant’ loosely or misplacing a unit changes the claim. The domain runs from accurate number expressions and approximation, through units and mathematical expression, to statistical vocabulary and consumer-level interpretation of statistical claims, drawing on research into statistical literacy (Gal, 2002) and risk communication (Gigerenzer et al., 2007). EAP teachers without statistical training may wish to co-teach the later topics with subject or mathematics-support colleagues.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to talk and write about numbers, measurements and statistics precisely, and to understand what statistical claims in your reading do and do not show.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Accurate number expressions and number style, units and basic statistical terms in subject modules such as mathematics, science and business, in speech and writing.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Precise and appropriately approximate figures in short data descriptions, and the everyday versus statistical senses of key terms.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Precision and approximation in data commentary, relative versus absolute change in sources, and statistical vocabulary met in research reading.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Discipline-specific notation and units, statistical vocabulary in methods and results, and reading statistical claims in sources.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Consumer-level interpretation of p-values, confidence intervals and effect sizes in research reading and dissertations.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Accurate statistical and mathematical expression in theses and articles, following field and journal conventions.

domains.name: Multimodal Composition
domains.summary: Academic communication increasingly combines writing with images, layout, colour, sound and movement, and university assessment now includes infographics, podcasts, video essays and e-portfolios. This domain treats multimodal composition as meaning-making with distinct semiotic resources (Kress & van Leeuwen, 2006), addresses the design of digital and visual-summary genres (Hafner, 2014), and treats accessibility as a design requirement from the outset rather than an afterthought (World Wide Web Consortium, 2023). Academic expectations of argument, evidence and attribution carry over into these genres even though the means of realising them change. Poster design is treated together with presenting posters in the presentations strand (prs.posters).
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how images, layout and text work together, and how to make infographics and digital assignments that are clear, persuasive and accessible to all your readers.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Awareness of how layout and images make meaning, developed through short digital tasks and simple visual summaries.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Analysing layout and image–text relations, and short recorded or digital presentations as assessed work.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Recorded or digital presentations as assessed work, with accessible document structure, alternative text and captions in submitted work.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Discipline-specific multimodal assessments (video essays, e-portfolios, infographics) and accessible document design.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Infographics for professional audiences, digital portfolios and accessible dissertation formatting.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Visual abstracts and public-engagement graphics, and accessibility in theses, publications and teaching materials.

domains.name: Self-Regulated Learning
domains.summary: This domain covers the knowledge and strategies that let learners direct their own academic and language development: metacognitive knowledge, self-regulation and learner autonomy, motivation, goal setting, time management, independent study, study techniques, language learning strategies, reflective logs, support services, wellbeing and learning content through English. It is anchored in self-regulated learning research (Zimmerman, 2002; Flavell, 1979), autonomy research (Holec, 1981; Benson, 2011) and cognitive research on durable learning (Dunlosky et al., 2013). The conceptual topics are taught explicitly mainly at foundation level and revisited later, while the strategic topics are best taught through learners' real tasks and evidence (feedback, self-test results, time logs) rather than as detached 'study skills'.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to plan, check and evaluate your own learning, choose study methods that work, manage your time and wellbeing, and keep improving your English after your course.

stageEmphasis.foundation: The main stage for explicit work on self-regulation and autonomy, independent study, evidence-informed study techniques and learning subject content through English, linked to the shift from school to university-style learning.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Compressed work on reflective logs, goal setting and study techniques tied to weekly tasks and the progression decision; the self-regulation model is revisited rather than retaught.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Reflective logs and goal setting linked to progression and to planning continued language development during a short, intensive master's year.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Revisited at transition points (first assessments, first exam season), mainly through time management, study techniques and learning disciplinary content in English.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid orientation to a dense one-year programme: workload planning, independent study expectations and learning disciplinary content and language together.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Largely revisited: doctoral self-management is addressed through supervision and thesis-writing topics, with wellbeing over long, isolated projects as the main remaining concern.

domains.name: Feedback & Assessment Literacy
domains.summary: This domain covers how learners come to understand university assessment and use feedback: assessment purposes and rules, grading systems, marking criteria, feedback literacy, acting on feedback, using written corrective feedback, seeking feedback and self- and peer-assessment. It draws on Sadler's (1989) argument that learners must come to share the assessor's concept of quality, on feedback as a support for self-regulation (Nicol & Macfarlane-Dick, 2006; Hattie & Timperley, 2007), on student feedback literacy (Carless & Boud, 2018) and on the contested evidence on written corrective feedback (Truscott, 1996; Ferris, 1999; Bitchener & Ferris, 2012; Kang & Han, 2015). Grading scales, feedback conventions and rules on pre-submission help differ between institutions and national systems, so topics are framed around the learner's target context rather than a single national model.
