In EMI and transnational programmes (see acu.emi-tne), learners may meet local and partner-institution conventions at once, such as two grading scales, or feedback practices that differ from those of an anglophone campus.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how university assessment works and what marking criteria and grades mean. You will also learn to ask for, understand and act on feedback so that each assignment improves the next.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Explicit introduction to formative and summative assessment, local grading conventions and criterion-referenced coursework, often the learner's first encounter with them.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Intensive use of rubrics, correction codes and draft–feedback cycles leading to the progression assessment, with explicit work on acting on language feedback.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Criteria, exemplars and draft–feedback cycles leading to progression, with emphasis on self- and peer-assessment to build the evaluative judgement that master's study expects.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Interpreting disciplinary criteria and feedback on early assignments, and building feed-forward habits across modules.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid calibration to master's-level standards and marking conventions, where marks may look lower than learners expect and feedback often arrives after the next assignment is due.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Seeking and negotiating feedback from supervisors, peers and reviewers, and developing the evaluative judgement needed to review one's own and others' research writing.

domains.name: Exams & Timed Performance
domains.summary: This domain covers university examinations and timed performance: understanding exam formats, planning revision, writing under time pressure, approaching objective-format questions, open-book, take-home and online time-windowed exams, oral examinations and managing test anxiety; analysing exam questions is taught within task analysis (wpr.task-analysis). It draws on cognitive research on retrieval and spacing (Dunlosky et al., 2013; Roediger & Karpicke, 2006), research on planning in L2 writing (Ellis & Yuan, 2004), writing assessment (Weigle, 2002) and test anxiety (Putwain, 2008; Horwitz et al., 1986). Emphasis is on matching preparation and in-exam behaviour to the demands of each format rather than on generic exam tips, and on the adjustments (extra time, rest breaks, assistive technology, alternative arrangements) that make timed formats accessible.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how university exams work, including open-book and online ones, how to revise so that you remember, how to write and speak well under time pressure, and how to manage exam nerves.

stageEmphasis.foundation: First experience of university-style exams in subject modules: formats, revision planning and timed writing, often alongside content learning in English.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Timed writing as part of progression, often in an integrated reading-into-writing task, with a preview of first-year exam formats and work on managing anxiety in high-stakes conditions.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Timed, online or oral tasks where the progression assessment uses them; exam work is lighter than on UG-route courses because many master's programmes assess mainly through coursework.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support before exam seasons: exam essays and short answers, revision planning, objective-format papers, and open-book, take-home or online time-windowed exams.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid preparation for unfamiliar formats (seen papers, take-home and case-based exams, online time-windowed papers) within a compressed year.

domains.name: Proficiency Tests & Progression
domains.summary: This domain helps learners understand the language assessments that control access to and progression through university study: the purposes of different assessments, CEFR levels and entry requirements, score reports and test choice, the task types and constructs of academic proficiency tests, the differences between test tasks and university tasks, and pre-sessional progression assessment; integrated reading- and listening-into-writing tasks, including their test versions, are taught in syn.integrated-tasks. It draws on language assessment theory (Bachman & Palmer, 2010; Weigle, 2002), the CEFR (Council of Europe, 2001, 2020; North, 2014) and research on test washback and on the gap between test and university writing (Green, 2007; Moore & Morton, 2005). Test formats, score-use rules and visa requirements change, and major tests have been redesigned in recent years, so content is framed at the level of task types and constructs, and learners are directed to current official sources.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn what language tests and progression assessments are for, how to read a score report, and how test tasks differ from university work.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Understanding entry and progression requirements, score reports and test formats, while building the broader academic literacy that tests only partly measure.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Central: understanding the progression assessment and how it relates to entry requirements, and moving from test-oriented habits towards first-year coursework.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Central: understanding the progression assessment, reading score reports and conditional offers, and moving from test tasks to source-based master's writing.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Addressing the move from test preparation to disciplinary writing, and the supportive purpose of post-entry diagnostic assessment.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid recalibration for direct entrants who must adjust from test tasks to source-based disciplinary writing within a year.

domains.name: Academic Culture & Expectations
domains.summary: Makes explicit how universities and disciplines are organised, what they expect of learners and how those expectations are communicated, often tacitly. The domain moves from orientation knowledge (structures, teaching formats, roles and address) through discourse-community and disciplinary awareness to making informed choices about conventions, and includes two teacher-facing principles (the academic literacies perspective, and designing for EMI and transnational contexts) that shape how the rest is taught. Difficulty is framed as a mismatch between practices, not a learner deficit, and tacit expectations affect first-generation, mature, part-time and widening-participation home students as well as international students. Structures, roles and expectations differ in EMI programmes and transnational branch campuses, where an awarding institution's regulations may sit alongside local academic culture (see acu.emi-tne).
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how your university and subject work and what is expected of you, including unwritten rules. You will also learn when and how to make your own informed choices.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Orientation to structures, teaching formats, roles and address, and stated expectations is core, taught through real institutional documents at the point of need; in EMI and TNE foundation programmes, learners also map how local and awarding-institution practices combine.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Orientation to the destination institution's structures, formats, address norms and stated expectations is core, with tacit expectations and transition support woven into language work rather than taught as separate sessions.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Orientation focuses on what changes at postgraduate level (seminar-based teaching, independence, compressed timelines), with a first comparison of disciplinary knowledge-making and discourse communities in mixed-discipline groups.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Decoding tacit expectations in the student's own modules is core, ideally co-taught with subject staff; provision increasingly serves home, first-generation and mature students, and in EMI and TNE programmes expectations are often set by content lecturers who do not see language as their remit.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid re-orientation within one-year programmes, disciplinary knowledge-making for students changing field, and exemplar-based work on tacit criteria.
stageEmphasis.pgr: No general orientation: the focus is doctoral tacit expectations (supervision, progression reviews, the viva), the researcher's place in disciplinary communities and informed choices about conventions in English-medium publishing.

domains.name: Academic Pragmatics & Correspondence
domains.summary: Covers the sociopragmatic and pragmalinguistic resources learners need to interact with staff, peers and employers outside the core academic genres: politeness and face, requests, apologies and accounts, emails, office hours, formal institutional statements, forum posts, channel choice, informal academic talk, and applications and interviews for placements and graduate roles. Interlanguage pragmatics research shows that pragmatic competence does not keep pace with grammatical development without attention, and that staff judge messages on perceived politeness and clarity as well as accuracy. Norms vary across institutions, countries and individuals, and in EMI and TNE settings forms of address, channels (including messaging apps) and procedures may follow local rather than anglophone conventions (see acu.emi-tne); the aim is informed, context-sensitive choice, not one correct formula.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to write emails, make requests, apologise and talk with staff and other students in ways that suit the situation. You will also practise forum posts, formal statements and job applications.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Emails, requests and forms of address are core, practised on real tasks such as contacting a tutor or reporting an absence, with informal talk with peers and staff supported rather than assumed.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Emails and requests to staff are core, calibrated to power, distance and imposition, with forum participation and office-hour rehearsal using the destination institution's channels.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Email to staff and prospective supervisors is core, alongside tutorial rehearsal and informal interaction with peers and department or lab colleagues.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Point-of-need application (extensions, feedback tutorials, assessed forums, extenuating circumstances) and, with careers services, placement applications; norms are checked locally, especially in EMI and TNE programmes.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Efficient correspondence and meetings within a compressed timeline, dissertation-related contact, and applications and interviews for graduate roles.
stageEmphasis.pgr: High-imposition requests to supervisors, gatekeepers and external researchers, multichannel professional communication, informal networking in departments, and academic and non-academic job applications.

domains.name: Identity, Plurilingualism & Intercultural Competence
domains.summary: This domain addresses who learners are as academic language users: how writing and speaking construct identity, how plurilingual repertoires can be used strategically from the start of study, when other languages and Englishes may appear in academic texts, how English functions as a lingua franca and in established World Englishes, and how intercultural and rhetorical differences can be understood without stereotyping. It adopts a resource rather than a deficit orientation, treats culture as dynamic, multiple and partly institutional, names native-speakerism and racialised language judgements, and presents contrastive rhetoric and language separation in assessed texts as contested. Several topics pair a learner skill with a curriculum principle for teachers (audience 'both'), and practice differs in EMI and transnational programmes, where other languages are often part of everyday study.
domains.learnerSummary: You will explore how your writing and speech present you and how to use all your languages as resources. You will also practise communicating across differences without stereotypes.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Start from learners' own languages: map and use plurilingual repertoires, collaborate inclusively in multilingual groups, and discuss in simple terms whose English counts and when other languages may appear in writing.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Address transition and emerging academic identity alongside lingua franca interaction in multilingual cohorts, and clarify when other languages may be used in assessed work.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Prepare for postgraduate study as multilingual scholars: use literatures in several languages, discuss native-speakerism and legitimacy, and begin to articulate a disciplinary identity.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support inclusive group work, emerging disciplinary voice and resource-oriented participation for home and international students alike, including first-generation and mature students.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Help highly international cohorts negotiate identity, intercultural collaboration and unfamiliar expectations within a short programme.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Focus on researcher identity, multilingual and translingual scholarship, publishing as a multilingual scholar and positioning within global scholarly communities.

domains.name: Digital Scholarship Tools
domains.summary: Academic work is mediated by digital tools (learning platforms, word processors, reference managers, shared documents, translation tools, editing and automated feedback tools, and assistive technologies) whose effective and ethical use is rarely taught explicitly. This domain treats these tools as part of academic literacy practices rather than as separate technical skills (Lea & Jones, 2011), emphasising critical and transparent use: tools support but do not replace learners’ judgement, their outputs must be checked, and their permitted use is set by institutional rules. Assistive technologies and study adjustments are treated as legitimate academic practice, and because products change quickly, topics are framed around transferable functions and decisions rather than named applications.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to use the digital tools of university study, including translation, editing and assistive tools, efficiently, critically and within your institution’s rules.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Orientation to the learning platform, files and word processing, built-in assistive features introduced to everyone, and transparent, critical use of translation tools.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Institutional systems, the rules on translation, editing and AI tools in progression assessments, versioned drafts for portfolios, and shared documents in group projects.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Rules on translation, editing and AI tools in progression assessments, an introduction to reference managers, and versioned drafts for an extended project.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Efficient assignment workflows: styles, reference managers, shared documents, module-specific tool rules and critical use of feedback tools.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Managing dissertation-scale work: versioning, reference libraries, collaboration and supervisor feedback in shared documents.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Thesis-scale documents and reference libraries, confidentiality when using online tools, adjustments for thesis submission and the viva, and a professional online presence.

domains.name: Generative AI Literacy
domains.summary: Generative AI literacy is treated here as part of academic literacy: understanding how large language models generate text and why they fail; reading and applying AI policies that vary by institution, module and task; acknowledging and verifying AI use; and using AI as a tutor and practice partner in ways that build rather than replace learners' own language, reasoning and voice. The domain also covers the limits of AI-text detection, including documented bias against writers using English as an additional language and why detector output cannot establish misconduct, the contested question of where AI assistance ends and authorship begins, and privacy and intellectual-property risks. Tools and policies change quickly, so topics are framed around durable principles and verification habits rather than particular products.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how AI tools work and fail, and what each task allows. You will practise declaring and checking AI use, learning with AI, and responding if a detector wrongly flags your work.

stageEmphasis.foundation: How generative AI works and fails, finding the AI rules for each task, and using AI for explanation and practice rather than to produce assessed text.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Finding and applying the AI rules for each pre-sessional task, declaring use honestly, and using AI to learn rather than to write assessed text.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: AI rules and declarations for postgraduate study, verifying AI-supplied references and summaries, and a first look at the research, privacy and authorship questions that arise in master's and doctoral work.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Module-specific rules, acknowledging use, and evaluating AI as a language and study resource within the discipline.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: AI in literature searching and summarising, authorship and voice in extended writing, and data privacy in dissertation research.
stageEmphasis.pgr: AI research tools, publisher and funder policies, research data privacy and intellectual property, and authorship norms in publication.

domains.name: Science, Engineering & Computing
domains.summary: This domain covers the discourse of the natural sciences, engineering, mathematics and computing: how technicality, grammatical metaphor and taxonomies build scientific knowledge, and how learners produce explanations, protocols and specifications, experimental language, research records, proofs and software documentation. These fields are typically hard disciplines in Becher and Trowler’s terms, with cumulative knowledge, high consensus on method and texts in which visuals, notation and code carry much of the meaning. Teaching works best when EAP staff analyse departmental exemplars with subject lecturers, because conventions differ between, for example, a chemistry protocol, a civil engineering specification and a computing README.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how scientists, engineers, mathematicians and programmers use English to explain, specify, prove, document and keep research records, and how to write these texts as your department expects.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Build control of scientific explanation and the language of science and experimentation alongside subject content, using textbook and practical-class texts.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: On science and engineering pathways for undergraduate entry, raise awareness of technicality and nominalisation and practise scientific explanation and experimental language.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: On pathways for science, engineering and computing master’s entrants, focus on reading dense research prose and on precise experimental language.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Embed work on experimental language, specifications, proofs and documentation in modules, ideally co-designed with subject staff around real assignments.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on research-project records, precision in specifications and design documentation, and the conventions of the student’s specialism.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Support research records and data management, protocol and methods writing, documentation of research software and the conventions of mathematical and technical publication.

domains.name: Health & Life Sciences
domains.summary: This domain covers the literacies of nursing, midwifery, medicine, allied health, pharmacy and related life-science programmes, where academic writing is tied to professional practice and patient safety. Its topics are evidence-based practice as an organising concept, writing clinical reasoning, care plans, case presentations, reflective practice writing, communication on placement and critical appraisal of research. Many of these genres are assessed against professional standards as well as academic criteria, so EAP teachers should work with clinical educators, use anonymised local exemplars and check regulator and programme requirements on confidentiality and record-keeping.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how health professionals use evidence, explain clinical reasoning, write care plans and reflections, present cases, appraise research and communicate safely with patients and colleagues.

stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: On health pathways for undergraduate entry, introduce reflective writing, evidence-based practice and the spoken patterns of patient communication before first placements.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: On pathways for health master’s entrants, many of them experienced practitioners, focus on evidence-based practice, reflective analysis and making professional reasoning explicit in academic prose.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Embed support for clinical reasoning, care plans, reflective assignments and placement communication in nursing, midwifery, medicine and allied-health programmes.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Emphasise critical appraisal, clinical reasoning in complex cases and analytical reflection for practitioners taking master’s degrees.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Doctoral researchers revisit appraisal as risk-of-bias assessment; systematic review writing is covered by the research-writing topics.

domains.name: Business & Economics
domains.summary: This domain covers the literacies of business, management, accounting, finance and economics programmes, which together attract the largest international cohorts on UG and PGT courses. Business schools assess many simulated or live professional genres (case analyses, reports, memos, pitches, consultancy reports) oriented to decision-makers, accounting and finance assess commentary on figures and disclosures, and economics builds arguments from models, assumptions and conditional reasoning. Nathan (2013) and Zhu (2004) show that these assignment genres differ from the academic essay in purpose, structure and reader, so EAP teaching should analyse the school’s own briefs and exemplars with subject staff.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to analyse business cases, use frameworks critically, reason with economic models, comment on financial results and write the reports your business school assesses.

stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: On business pathways for undergraduate entry, contrast case analysis and the business report with the essay, and practise applying frameworks to short cases with evidence.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: On pathways for business, finance and economics master’s entrants, practise case and framework analysis, financial commentary and decision-oriented reports at the pace of a one-year degree.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Embed support for case analyses, reports and economic reasoning in modules, using the school’s own briefs and exemplars.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Support the high volume of case-based, financial and consultancy genres on master’s programmes such as the MBA, MSc Management and MSc Finance, where students have little time to adjust.

domains.name: Law
domains.summary: This domain covers the literacies of studying law in English, with a primary focus on common-law systems such as England and Wales: the register and terms of art of legal English, reading and briefing cases, reading legislation, answering problem questions, writing legal essays, arguing orally in moots and writing law dissertations. Legal knowledge is constructed through authoritative texts (judgments and statutes) whose language is itself the object of analysis, so reading precision and the handling of authority are central (Bhatia, 1993; Twining & Miers, 2010), and doctrinal research has its own method (Hutchinson & Duncan, 2012). Many international law students, especially on LLM programmes, trained in civil-law or mixed systems, which makes it particularly important to make common-law conventions explicit.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to read cases and legislation, use legal terms precisely, answer problem questions, write legal essays and dissertations, and argue orally in moots.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Introduce legal vocabulary and the idea of precedent in law foundation programmes.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: On law pathways for LLB entry, practise reading short judgments and statutes and contrast problem questions with essays.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: On pathways for LLM entrants, many trained in civil-law systems, make reasoning from precedent explicit and introduce legal essays, OSCOLA and dissertation method.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Embed support for case briefing and problem questions in first-year LLB modules, where the conventions are new to everyone, and for mooting later.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Support LLM students in reading common-law materials efficiently and writing analytical legal essays and dissertations with OSCOLA referencing.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Support doctoral law researchers in stating their method and sustaining doctrinal or socio-legal argument across a thesis.

domains.name: Social Sciences & Education
domains.summary: This domain covers the literacies of sociology, politics, social policy, international relations, psychology, education and related fields. Key concepts are often contested, several research paradigms coexist and writers are expected to justify their conceptual and methodological choices explicitly, while psychology combines this with the tightly conventionalised experimental report and education with practice genres such as lesson-plan rationales and teaching reflections. The topics address working with contested concepts, justifying methodology, the process texts of qualitative research, policy analysis, psychology reports and education practice genres, which recur from UG coursework to doctoral theses. Because expectations vary between fields and between supervisors, analysis of local exemplars with subject staff is essential.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to define contested concepts, justify your methods, keep qualitative field notes, write psychology reports and teaching documents, and analyse policy.

stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: On social science pathways for undergraduate entry, introduce contested concepts and the idea that definitions must be justified.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: On pathways for social science, psychology and education master’s entrants, introduce contested concepts and the expectation that methods are justified, and practise the rationale and reflective genres of teacher education.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support concept work, psychology reports, policy analysis and the methods of final-year projects.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on methodology chapters, qualitative analysis, policy analysis and TESOL and education practice genres in master’s programmes, where many students are new to the paradigms of the field.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Support doctoral researchers in articulating paradigms, operationalising concepts and accounting for extended qualitative analysis.

domains.name: Humanities
domains.summary: This domain covers the literacies of literary studies, history, philosophy, religious studies, classics and related fields, where knowledge is built through interpretation and argument about texts, sources and ideas rather than through accumulating findings. Becher and Trowler characterise these 'soft-pure' fields as reiterative and interpretive, and Hyland (2004) shows that their writing typically has more explicit authorial presence and evaluative engagement with sources than the sciences. The topics cover close reading, working with primary sources, interpretive argument and philosophical writing, all of which reward detailed engagement with language and a sustained individual voice.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to analyse texts closely, work with primary sources, argue for an interpretation with evidence and write philosophical arguments with objections and replies.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Introduce close reading and the use of quotation as evidence on humanities foundation programmes.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: On humanities pathways for undergraduate entry, practise close analysis of short texts and the shift from summary to interpretation.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: On pathways for humanities master’s entrants, practise positioning an interpretation within critical or historiographical debate.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support close reading and interpretive essays in subject modules, using the department’s exemplars.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Emphasise original interpretation, engagement with critical debates and archival or primary-source work for dissertations.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Support doctoral researchers in sustaining interpretive arguments across chapters and in archival research and citation.

domains.name: Creative Arts & Design
domains.summary: This domain covers the literacies of fine art, design (graphic, product, fashion, interior), architecture, performance and related practice-based programmes, where much learning takes place in the studio and assessment centres on work produced, presented and explained. Language does specific jobs here: describing and interpreting visual work, presenting and defending work in critiques, writing statements and rationales that make practice legible to tutors, audiences and juries, and, at master’s and doctoral level, writing the exegesis that argues the research contribution of a practice. Schön’s (1983) account of design as a reflective conversation with materials and Kress and van Leeuwen’s (2006) visual grammar give EAP teachers ways to describe these practices, but the tacit vocabulary of a studio is local, so close collaboration with studio tutors and observation of crits is recommended.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to describe and discuss visual work, present in studio crits, and write statements, rationales and research texts that explain your practice.

stageEmphasis.foundation: On art and design foundation courses, build vocabulary for visual analysis, sketchbook annotation and confidence in presenting work in crits.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: On art and design pathways for undergraduate entry, practise describing visual work and presenting it in short simulated crits.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: On pathways for art and design master’s entrants, practise articulating an existing practice in statements and introduce writing about practice as research.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support crit participation and design rationales in studio modules, ideally with tutors present.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on articulating a practice in relation to context and theory in statements, rationales, final crits and critical reports.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Support practice-based doctoral researchers with the exegesis: method through making, contextualisation and claims of contribution.
